chief_complaint: painful erections and progressive 45-degree upward curvature of penis with palpable hard plaque
hpi_details: 52M presenting with painful erections and progressive 45-degree dorsal angulation during tumescence that impairs intercourse, with a palpable fibrous plaque of the tunica albuginea. He is seeking evaluation and a discussion of treatment options.
ideas: He thinks he bent or tore internal tissue during intercourse a few months ago and it healed into a stiff, crooked scar.
concerns: He is worried that the hard lump is a cancerous tumor or that his intimacy with his wife is permanently over.
expectations: He hopes to be prescribed a pill or an injection that can dissolve the hard lump and straighten the curve without surgery.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Peyronie Disease Penile Curvature evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Peyronie Disease Penile Curvature is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Management depends on phase, degree of deformity, erectile function, and bother; pain and curvature may evolve during the active phase before stabilizing.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painful erections and progressive 45-degree upward curvature of penis with palpable hard plaque
Key HPI features: painful erections, progressive 45-degree dorsal curvature, palpable plaque, and intercourse impairment.
Objective/Exam findings: Document plaque location, stretched penile length, curvature/deformity, and erectile function; erection photographs or in-office induced erection may help quantify deformity.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Peyronie Disease Penile Curvature.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing penile fracture when there is a sudden snap, immediate detumescence, swelling/bruising, or urethral bleeding after trauma.
Offering collagenase without counseling about bruising/hematoma and the rare risk of corporal rupture, or without confirming appropriate candidacy.
management_principles: In the active painful phase, provide reassurance, address distress and erectile dysfunction, and consider NSAID analgesia if safe for the patient.

For stable, bothersome curvature, discuss traction therapy, intralesional collagenase for selected men with a palpable plaque, 30–90 degree curvature, and adequate erectile function, or surgery after disease stability.
Tailor surgery: plication for less complex curvature with adequate length/erections; incision/grafting or penile prosthesis for selected complex deformity or refractory erectile dysfunction.
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 52M with painful erections, progressive 45-degree dorsal curvature, palpable plaque, and impaired intercourse; he requests evaluation and treatment options.
reference_soap.objective: Examine for plaque, quantify curvature and deformity, document stretched penile length and erectile function; use patient photographs or induced erection assessment if needed.
reference_soap.assessment: Likely Peyronie disease, apparently in the active phase because pain and progression are reported.
reference_soap.plan: Refer to urology/sexual-medicine specialist. Clarify duration/stability and erectile function; offer pain control if appropriate and counseling. Once curvature is stable and bothersome, discuss traction, selected-candidate collagenase, or individualized surgery. Seek emergency care after traumatic snap, immediate detumescence, marked swelling, or urethral bleeding.

teaching.one_liner: Urology evaluation for patient presenting with painful erections and progressive 45-degree upward curvature of penis with palpable hard plaque.
differentials: Cavernosal fibrosis from prior priapism or injection
red_flags: Sudden snap or bend during intercourse with immediate detumescence, swelling, bruising, or urethral bleeding (possible penile fracture)
Painful erection lasting more than four hours (possible priapism)

must_ask.objective: Onset and progression of the curvature
must_ask.say: When did you first notice the curve, and has it been getting worse or has it stayed the same recently?

must_ask.objective: Pain with erection and palpable plaque
must_ask.say: Do you have pain during erections, and can you feel a hard lump or band along the shaft?

must_ask.objective: Impact on erectile function and intercourse
must_ask.say: Is the curve severe enough to make sex difficult or painful for you or your partner?

must_ask.objective: History of penile trauma or vigorous intercourse injury
must_ask.say: Do you remember any specific injury or 'bending' incident to your penis before this started?

must_ask.objective: Explore emotional impact and treatment expectations
must_ask.say: How has this been affecting you emotionally, and what are you hoping we can do about it?

history.answer: Doctor, my penis curves upward when I get an erection, and it has become quite painful.
It started about four months ago. At first it was very slight, but over the last couple of months the bend has gradually become much more noticeable.
When I have a full erection, it bends upward toward my stomach at about a forty-five-degree angle.
About three months ago, I noticed a firm, hard spot on the top side of the shaft that feels like a small flattened lump under the skin.
It aches right along the top of the shaft where that hard spot is whenever I get an erection. When my penis is limp, there is no pain at all.
During an erection, the pain is a dull, tight ache, around a four or five out of ten in severity.
Erections always bring on the pain and make the bend obvious. Once the erection goes down, the pain stops completely.
Because of the upward curve and the discomfort, vaginal penetration has become very difficult and painful for both my wife and me.
I am still able to achieve an erection, but the pain and curvature make it hard to maintain rigidity and enjoy intimacy.
No, I never experienced any sudden snap, severe bend, or obvious trauma during intercourse.
No, there was never any sudden popping sound, rapid swelling, or purple bruising on my penis.
No, I have never had an erection that lasted for hours or refused to go down.
No, I have not noticed any bleeding, discharge, or sores from the tip of my penis.
No, I have no pain or burning when I urinate, no blood in my urine, and no changes in my urinary stream.
No, I have not had any fevers, chills, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss.
No, my penis was always completely straight before this, and I have never experienced anything like this in the past.
I took ibuprofen a few times when the ache was bothersome, which helped slightly, but I have not used any other medications, devices, or supplements.
I think I must have bent or torn something during sex a while back and it just scarred up stiff and crooked.
I'm terrified this hard lump might be a tumor, or that my sex life with my wife is over for good.
I'm hoping there's a pill or an injection that can dissolve this lump and straighten things out without needing an operation.
It has been emotionally distressing and frustrating for me, and it has put a strain on our intimacy as a couple.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers or glasses of wine on the weekend.
I work as an accountant in an office, live with my wife, and maintain an active lifestyle with regular exercise.
There is no family history of penile curvature, Dupuytren's contracture, or other connective tissue disorders.
I have been in a mutually monogamous relationship with my wife for over twenty years, with no history of sexually transmitted infections.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Well-appearing, alert man in no acute physical distress sitting comfortably on the examination table.
Soft, non-tender abdomen without masses, organomegaly, or suprapubic fullness.

Normal male external genitalia; palpation of the flaccid penile shaft reveals a firm, well-demarcated fibrous plaque measuring approximately 1.5 cm on the dorsal mid-shaft tunica albuginea without erythema, skin lesions, or urethral discharge.
No inguinal hernia or significant inguinal lymphadenopathy detected bilaterally.
Normal skin turgor without systemic rashes, nodules, or palmar fascial thickening on either hand.
